items.summary: On November 24, Alibaba rejected the addition of its subsidiary Apex Enterprise Solutions (Singapore) to a United States trade blacklist, calling it an "erroneous" move. In a statement provided to The Straits Times, an Alibaba spokesperson said that adding Apex to the Entity List is erroneous because "Apex has never diverted advanced computing chips subject to US export restrictions," and added that the company will pursue all legal avenues to protect its rights and reputation. Apex was one of seven companies added on November 23 to an entity list managed by the United States Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which said the firms were "determined by the US government to be acting contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States." Singapore-based Megaspeed International, at the centre of investigations into possible diversion of advanced Nvidia chips to China, was the primary target; its parent company Swiftdata and Malaysian subsidiaries MSFusion, Speedmatrix and Megaspeed International, plus Thai subsidiary Megaspeed (Thailand), were also blacklisted. Corporate records obtained by The Straits Times earlier in November showed Apex had an active financial arrangement with Speedmatrix under a June 18, 2024 agreement pledging specified IT and network equipment, intellectual property and related rights as security for contractual obligations; corporate records also show Apex was incorporated in Singapore in July 2023 at Lazada One on Bras Basah Road, leased by Alibaba and its Southeast Asian online shopping unit Lazada Group. Alibaba's immediate holding company is Cloud Intelligence (Cayman) Holding, with ultimate control held by Cayman Islands-incorporated Alibaba Group Holding, which holds contractual rights to Alibaba China's profits.
items.title: Alibaba Rejects US Blacklisting of Singapore Chip-Rerouting Subsidiary

items.summary: Meta launched its personal AI agent, Muse, in the UK today (the article states it 'rolls out in the UK today'), positioning agents as systems that carry out tasks rather than merely answering questions. Meta has made an enormous bet on this technology: of the $145bn it will spend this year, much of it is earmarked for building out AI tech, with hopes that Muse becomes the dominant choice for billions—comparable to what WhatsApp did for messaging.
items.title: Meta's AI Agent Muse Launches in the UK Amid Privacy Concerns and a $145 Billion Bet

items.summary: North Carolina's five-member, Republican-controlled Utilities Commission declined to order Duke Energy to file or propose a clean customer (clean transition) tariff in its Nov. 16 regulatory order, instead only encouraging the vertically integrated monopoly utility to collaborate with interested parties and voluntarily pursue such a program. The decision came despite heightened attention from large corporate electricity buyers seeking special rate structures that would let them contract for their own renewable electrons through Duke without violating state law; tech firms and other big consumers have long sought this arrangement because they can otherwise buy power only from the monopoly utility, which has not followed through on clean tariff plans since spring 2024. Steve Levitas of New Energy Economics, who testified before the commission for the Corporate Energy Buyers Association's 300-plus members, welcomed the language but called it insufficient, noting interveners had simply asked that Duke be required to file a voluntary customer program and arguing such clean electrons could have connected to the grid without them. The snub arrived on the same day regulators approved Duke's request to raise household rates by about 9.5% over two years and establish special terms of service for data centers, which advocates say should pay directly for their generation rather than shifting costs to ratepayers; meanwhile, Duke's existing Green Source Advantage Choice programs have largely flopped with no large customer applying for its resource acceleration option. Public Staff, the state-sanctioned customer advocate, also raised doubts about designing such a program and protecting average customers from footing the bill for expensive solar projects, critiques the commission reiterated in last week's order even as it pointed to similar clean transition tariffs enacted elsewhere, including Nevada where Google helped enact one. Commissioner Floyd McKissick expressed optimism that Duke and stakeholders could craft a proposal warranting serious consideration despite Green Source Advantage's failures, while midterm elections have renewed hopes that Democrats—now controlling the state House next year and nearly reaching Senate majority—with Gov. Josh Stein's bipartisan energy-policy task force expected to issue proposals in February, might require a clean tariff through legislation rather than relying on Duke's discretion.
items.title: North Carolina utility regulators punt on clean transition tariff — again

items.summary: The Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission (MERC) approved tariffs in its November 23, 2026 order under Case No. 218 of 2026 for the Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited (MSEDCL) to procure 2,000 MW/4,000 MWh of battery energy storage capacity over a 15-year period. The commission set monthly tariffs at Rs. 2,40,000 per MW for Part-A and Rs. 2,38,000 per MW for Part-B, with procurement supported through Viability Gap Funding (VGF) under the Power System Development Fund (PSDF). The approved projects will operate on a one-cycle-per-day basis with two-hour discharge durations.
items.title: MERC Approves Tariffs for MSEDCL's 2,000 MW/4,000 MWh Battery Storage Procurement

items.summary:
The Uttar Pradesh Electricity Regulatory Commission (UPERC) approved power procurement agreements and tariffs for 375 MW/1,500 MWh of standalone battery energy storage system (BESS) projects in Uttar Pradesh through orders dated November 19, 2026. Developed with viability gap funding (VGF) support under the Power System Development Fund (PSDF), the projects are expected to strengthen electricity supply management, support renewable energy integration, and improve grid stability. The storage will be supplied on demand for 15 years from each project's commercial operation date, with a scheduled commissioning of December 7, 2027 and VGF support of Rs. 18 lakh per MWh.

The procurement process attracted 13 bidders, of which 12 qualified during technical evaluation; eleven then participated in the electronic reverse auction conducted on May 2, 2026. UPPCL allocated the total capacity among three successful bidders based on lowest discovered tariffs and an applicable bucket-filling mechanism.

Under Petition No. 2404 of 2026, UPERC approved a tariff of Rs. 6.45 per kWh for KCC BESS Private Limited (a special purpose vehicle of KCC Buildcon Private Limited), which will develop an 187.5 MW/750 MWh standalone battery storage project and whose power procurement agreement with UPPCL was signed on June 1, 2026. Under Petition No. 2405 of 2026, the commission approved the same Rs. 6.45 per kWh tariff for Agastya Solar UP1 Private Limited (a subsidiary of Agastya Green Energy Limited), awarded 62.50 MW/250 MWh under an agreement dated June 8, 2026. Petition No. 2403 of 2026 involved the 125 MW/500 MWh project for MKC Kashivisvanath Ji Energy Private Limited (a subsidiary of MKC Green Energy Limited), which received a slightly higher tariff of Rs. 6.46 per kWh with an agreement signed on June 3, 2026.

UPPCL reported that the discovered tariffs of Rs. 6.45 and Rs. 6.46 per kWh were competitive versus previous procurement benchmarks, citing its earlier procurement through NTPC Vidyut Vyapar Nigam Limited (NVVN), where tariffs ranged between Rs. 6.71 and Rs. 6.72 per kWh; the new rates therefore represent a lower procurement cost for the approved storage capacity.

During the hearing held on October 1, 2026, UPERC raised concerns over UPPCL's failure to initially submit complete bidding documents with its petitions and directed the corporation to provide missing records. UPPCL subsequently apologized and submitted the required documents through an additional affidavit filed on October 23, 2026. After reviewing the records, bidding process, and applicable guidelines, the commission found that procurement followed the approved competitive bidding framework and consequently approved the discovered tariffs and power procurement agreements for all three projects.

The approved battery storage capacity is expected to help Uttar Pradesh manage peak electricity demand, improve renewable energy utilization, and provide greater grid flexibility. UPERC directed concerned parties to take timely action to ensure the projects meet their scheduled commissioning deadline of December 7, 2027.
items.title: UPERC Approves 375 MW/1,500 MWh Battery Storage Projects at Tariffs of INR 6.45–6.46 per kWh in Uttar Pradesh

items.summary: Utah City, a transit-oriented development rising on 700 acres in Vineyard, Utah — the former site of the defunct Geneva Steel complex — has opened its first two apartment buildings (120 and 220 Bend) with only about 1,400 rental units completed as of this summer. Primary developer Flagborough LLC describes it as a pedestrian-focused alternative to suburban sprawl, featuring the Greenline promenade connecting FrontRunner train station to Utah Lake.
items.title: Flagborough's Transit-Oriented Utah City Development Faces New Political Scrutiny

items.summary: The Iran war has cut phosphate fertilizer supplies by about 40 percent and raised prices beyond the reach of many farmers, while also reducing nitrogen-based ammonia supply to roughly a quarter. This disruption stems from the conflict's damage to Gulf production plants and closure of the Strait of Hormuz — the main shipping route for sulfur markets but not pipelines carrying solid sulfur — which cut off about 45 percent of worldwide trade in elemental sulfur, an essential feedstock derived largely from oil and gas refining rather than mining. Today more than 95 percent of global sulfur comes from refineries, a legacy of international efforts over three decades ago to scrub sulfur dioxide emissions that caused acid rain; those clean-up measures flooded the market with cheap waste sulfur, driving mine prices down about 80 percent and forcing mines in Sicily, Mexico, and Texas out of business. As a result, only two small mines remain open — Osiek Mine in Poland and Kawah Ijen volcano on Java's island — neither able to quickly scale up production.
items.title: Iran War Disrupts Fossil-Fuel-Dependent Global Phosphate Supply Chain

items.summary:
Despite midterm elections that progressives framed as victories over for-profit utilities, voters in two communities rejected proposals to replace investor-owned power companies with publicly owned ones. In both cases, private utilities spent roughly $2 million on opposition campaigns using similar messaging about costs and risks, and the measures failed by narrow margins.

In Kitsap County, Washington (population ~280,000), Puget Sound Energy's average power bill has nearly doubled over five years, with a proposed series of increases totaling 32 percent through 2029. The county utility district submitted a ballot initiative to take over power service from the company without an official feasibility study first; if it passed, commissioners would fund and conduct the study before proceeding. Puget Sound Energy's opposition campaign, "Too Costly. Too Risky. No Plan," spent $2.3 million — one of the most expensive local ballot fights in Washington history — while the district was prohibited from advocating for its own measure. The grassroots group Unplug PSE advocated with a budget of only $9,000. Puget Sound Energy argued that a buyout would be costly, citing demands during Jefferson County's earlier negotiations for $109 million for power lines and transformers (more than double assessed value), after which the company was ordered to return nearly $53 million in excess proceeds. The proposition received 42 percent approval.

In Ann Arbor, Michigan (~125,000 residents), a ballot proposal sought to establish a board to lead a transition away from DTE Energy and eventually replace it with a city-owned utility. DTE spent $1.8 million through the Ann Arbor Responsible Energy Coalition against the measure, arguing public power would be "too costly and too risky" and could impose up to $1 billion in debt on residents (a 2023 feasibility study estimated buyout costs between $281 million and $1.15 billion). The proposal failed by a margin of 3.6 percent, or 2,003 votes.

The article notes that both measures lacked full financial details ahead of voting, which supporters say weakened them; Kitsap County general manager Angela Bennink described creating new public utilities today as "fundamentally different" from the 1930s due to billion-dollar buyouts and well-funded opposition. Bonneville Power's cheap hydropower resources are stretched thin enough that a second county utility could claim available capacity first, potentially leaving Kitsap facing similar market challenges. Meanwhile, Milwaukee voted unanimously this month to fund a $1.35 million feasibility study for replacing investor-owned We Energies with a city utility; in Ann Arbor, an ambitious statewide measure amending campaign finance laws passed overwhelmingly.
items.title: Voters Reject Public Power in Ann Arbor and Kitsap County

items.summary: New research finds that residential solar installations can mitigate the mortality risks associated with extremely hot temperatures. Researchers Yi-Chun Ko of the Asian Growth Research Institute and Shinsuke Uchida of Japan's Doshisha University explored how household solar makes electricity more affordable to run air conditioning when prices spike due to supply disruptions, geopolitical shocks, or extreme heat.
items.title: Residential solar linked to reduced health risks from extreme temperatures

items.summary:
An international research team conducted a year-long experimental study assessing how bird droppings affect photovoltaic (PV) system performance, finding that soiling losses stabilize after prolonged accumulation and persist despite repeated rainfall events. Corresponding author Leonardo Micheli of the University of Split told pv magazine that the paper highlights this limitation but cannot yet provide a solution, noting that factors such as bird activity and proximity to nesting areas likely influence soiling accumulation and that further research is needed to identify quantitative variables for reliably modeling it. The study was published in Solar Energy under the title “Mind the birds: Assessing the uncertainty in modelling of urban photovoltaic soiling,” with a team including scientists from the University of Split, Croatia, and Sapienza University of Rome, Italy.

The experimental setup used two monocrystalline JA Solar JAM54S30-410/MR silicon modules installed at ground level on an open rack with identical tilt, azimuth, and height to ensure comparable environmental and irradiance conditions. Researchers conducted weekly measurements from July 2024 to July 2025, recording four current-voltage (I-V) curves per module using an EKO Instruments MP-11 tracer while measuring irradiance and module temperature near solar noon under clear skies in accordance with IEC 61724-1. They calculated the soiling ratio by comparing short-circuit currents of the soiled and clean modules, tested an alternative approach estimating clean-module output from irradiance and temperature data, and evaluated three established soiling models based on particulate matter concentrations and rainfall.

The researchers recorded an average soiling ratio of 0.941 over the monitoring period, corresponding to performance losses of approximately 6%, or about 72.1 kWh/kWp annually. The ratio fell below 0.90 in November 2024 following a prolonged dry period with bird droppings as the main contamination source; subsequent rainfall events only partially restored module performance, stabilizing the soiling ratio at around 0.94 to 0.96. A second accumulation period in April and May 2025 reduced the ratio to approximately 0.90, resulting in estimated daily energy losses of about 0.41 kWh/kWp and 0.47 kWh/kWp respectively.

The researchers found that only manual cleaning fully restored module performance, and their analysis showed the three conventional soiling models systematically underestimated losses because they relied primarily on particulate matter concentrations and assumptions about rainfall-induced cleaning. They concluded existing models cannot adequately capture bird-dropping accumulation and removal, particularly in urban environments, recommending additional soiling measurements, more detailed rainfall characteristics, and saturation effects for future models.
items.title: Study Finds Rainfall Cannot Fully Remove Bird-Dropping Soiling on Solar Panels

items.summary:
Equinor has signed an 18-year natural gas supply agreement with Germany's energy firm VNG, announced Tuesday—the longest gas sales contract the Norwegian company has secured since its agreements from 186. Under the deal, Equinor will deliver up to 15.3 TWh (around 1.4 billion cubic meters) of gas annually starting January 1, 2027, with deliveries continuing through the end of 2044 at Trading Hub Europe on market terms; other commercial details remain confidential between the parties.

Germany is Equinor's largest natural gas market and has served as an anchor for Norwegian gas exports since they began in 1977. VNG stated that the agreement strengthens its long-term portfolio while contributing to secure, diversified supplies in Germany, with CEO Ulf Heitmüller noting that "Norwegian pipeline gas remains of great importance for a reliable supply of energy to Germany and Europe." Earlier this year, Equinor signed a separate 15-year deal with Uniper covering more than 30 TWh annually through 2041.

The agreement aligns with Norway's goal to maintain high oil and gas production and exports for at least another decade. Since Russia cut off most of its European gas following the invasion of Ukraine, Norway has become the EU's single largest gas supplier and remains Europe's biggest supplier to the UK. Separately, Equinor plans to drill 20 to 30 exploration wells annually as it aims to sustain current production levels through at least 2035; in January, the company was awarded 35 new production licenses on the Norwegian continental shelf during Norway's tender for mature exploration areas.
items.title: Equinor Signs Longest Gas Supply Deal in 40 Years with Germany's VNG

items.summary:
Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO triggered a sharp rally across Asia-Pacific markets, with the Taiwanese TW50 index up 9.5%, South Korea's Kospi jumping 6.5% (led by SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics), Tokyo's Nikkei gaining nearly 4%, and Australia's S&P/ASX 200 rising 1.8%. This followed a Wall Street surge where Nvidia shares jumped 31.5%, adding roughly $950bn to the company's value as Huang returned to headquarters, marking Wall Street's best day since April 2025 when Trump paused his Liberation Day tariffs. Saxo chief investment strategist Charu Chanana attributed part of the rally to Huang's return removing uncertainty and restoring strategic continuity at Nvidia.

Despite the optimism, doubts persisted over AI companies' high valuations and whether they could generate revenues to sustain heavy data center spending. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index dipped 0.73%, which AJ Bell investment director Russ Mould suggested may reflect fears of a clampdown on US AI chip exports once the initial excitement faded.

Political backlash intensified, with Democrat Senator Elizabeth Warren calling Huang's restoration "reckless" and warning her upcoming banking committee would investigate whether Nvidia complied with export controls, while demanding Congress be told what input government officials gave to support his reinstatement. Republican lawmakers also criticized the board decision; Nebraska Senator Pete Ricketts wrote on X that Huang's behavior did not support reinstatement amid allegations of an affair with a Chinese spy.

Trump had reportedly dialed into Nvidia's Sunday board meeting before the announcement, arguing for Huang's return and asking Vice President JD Vance to work with the board to assure them Huang was not a national security risk. House Oversight Committee top Democrat Robert Garcia said Trump's direct involvement raised "serious national security and corruption questions," demanding swift bipartisan action.

Trump's Nvidia holdings rose in value by as much as $15m (£11.5m) on Monday, with his total stock position valued between $11m (£8.4m) and $55m (£42.1m), per the FT citing a Reuters review of disclosure filings.

Germany's foreign minister Johann Wadephul told AFP he was "shocked" by Trump's intervention to reinstate Huang, noting he had never seen such political interference in a company before. Chinese state media warned Beijing and Washington tensions would not end with Huang's return; Global Times urged China to remain vigilant against renewed export license delays and congressional hearings.

The Commerce Department added Megaspeed International to its trade blacklist on Monday, barring it from buying advanced AI chips without approval—a move that revealed Huang's relationship with Megaspeed founder Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing. Huang returned to Nvidia HQ wearing his signature dark uniform as employees chanted "Jensen, Jensen, Jensen," vowing to be a better CEO.

European markets showed less enthusiasm; London's FTSE 100 dipped 5 points (0.05%) to 10,475 after already rising 1.3% on Monday following the announcement. Swissquote senior analyst Ipek Ozkardeskaya noted Huang's return would not ease broader AI risks including massive infrastructure spending and hyperscaler free cash flow pressure.

Analysts offered mixed outlooks: UniCredit Munich strategist Christian Stocker said investors were re-engaging with the AI theme on relief that supply chain disruption was unlikely, while DeutscheBank's Jim Reid argued markets now priced in a more hawkish Federal Reserve path—with 25bp hike fully expected at December's meeting (26.1bps total, +3.1bps intraday) and 70bps of hikes by September 2027 (+6.6bps).
items.title: Nvidia shares fall in premarket trading as Jensen Huang’s return sparks US political backlash

items.summary: Nearly two weeks after Jensen Huang stepped down as chief executive of Nvidia, the Taiwanese-American tech billionaire was reinstated on Monday (Nov 23), sending Nvidia shares soaring 31.5 per cent in a day and reviving investor interest across AI-related stocks. The comeback followed revelations that had plunged the chipmaker into crisis: reports of extramarital affairs—including one with Alice Huang, suspected of being a Chinese spy—and mounting pressure from US President Donald Trump, industry figures like Tesla CEO Elon Musk, and prominent venture capitalists who signed an online petition drawing over 180,000 signatures. In his statement, Huang said he was honored to return and 'can't wait to get back to work,' while videos circulating on social media showed him wearing a navy jacket instead of his signature black leather jacket with his hand over his heart amid cheers from employees across multiple floors; he added that he would be 'a better CEO the second time around.' The timeline traces how the controversy unfolded, beginning Oct 29 when the New York Times reported US authorities investigated Alice Huang for allegedly passing intelligence to Beijing and helping circumvent restrictions on advanced AI chips—after which Nvidia's closing share price fell to US$213.66 (0.8 per cent down from Oct 28). On Oct 30, the Wall Street Journal alleged Alice Huang had links to Chinese intelligence, prompting Singapore officials' concerns; that day Huang told Bloomberg News his dealings with Megaspeed were 'normal and not unusual,' while Beijing dismissed the espionage claims as 'groundless speculation.' Trump voiced support on Oct 31, calling Huang 'brilliant' and saying Washington was looking 'very closely' at the issue. On Nov 4 to Nov 5, three senior Republican lawmakers requested a closed-door briefing from Huang over the intelligence allegations; Nvidia responded that its cloud customers in Asia receive ordinary business information rather than sensitive trade secrets or national security data, with closing shares falling to US$181.60 (9.3 per cent down from Nov 4). On Nov 8, Huang admitted his infidelity in a message to employees, taking 'full responsibility' while remaining committed to Nvidia and supporting the independent investigation; following this admission, Nvidia announced its board was launching an inquiry into whether Huang was targeted by foreign intelligence—though shares had already dropped about US$190 billion off market value—and closed at US$186.64 on Friday (Nov 6), up 2.8 per cent from Nov 5. On Nov 9, Trump defended Huang as an 'honorable guy' who had not discussed the affair allegations with him; Chinese officials again dismissed espionage claims during a press briefing, and Nvidia's closing share price fell to US$178.67 (4.3 per cent down from Nov 6). On Nov 10, The Associated Press reported that a shareholder sued Nvidia and Huang for deceiving investors about the affair and Megaspeed; shares closed at US$168.89 (5.5 per cent down from Nov 9). On Nov 11, the New York Times reported an alleged second affair with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care—while unconfirmed, this sent Nvidia shares falling nearly 4 per cent in extended trading; closing price rose to US$173.73 (2.9 per cent up from Nov 10). On Nov 12, Huang announced his resignation as CEO, with CFO Colette Kress taking over as interim chief executive and longtime engineer Ian Buck emerging as a leading internal candidate. On Nov 13, US lawmakers summoned Huang to face questions in December after the scandal had wiped almost half a trillion dollars off Nvidia's market valuation; Senator Tim Scott requested testimony before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec 1, while Huang faced closed-door interviews with three House committees under threat of subpoena—closing shares fell to US$162.85 (2 per cent down from Nov 12). On Nov 16, citing people familiar with the matter, the Financial Times reported Huang was considering a comeback as CEO; sources said Silicon Valley executives were assembling a 'war room' to lobby for his return and garner White House support, while Trump told reporters he would welcome Huang's return. However, on Nov 17, Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said the board did not intend to reinstate Huang despite his readiness to return—though Nvidia doubled its revenue in Q3 to more than US$115 billion, exceeding analysts' expectations; closing shares fell slightly to US$155.46 (0.4 per cent down from Nov 16). On Nov 20, Anthropic's record US$81 billion listing failed to arrest Nvidia's slide amid worries about the sector's investments and valuations, while Trump again praised Huang as 'a good man' who should be given a second chance; closing shares fell sharply to US$125.53 (14 per cent down from Nov 19). Finally on Nov 23, Nvidia's board reinstated Huang in a surprise move after late Sunday discussions that even interim CEO Colette Kress was unaware of—Jones said the board believed Jensen 'is the right person to lead Nvidia' and his return serves stockholders; despite gaining nearly US$1 trillion in market value, Nvidia remained worth about a fifth less than a month earlier.
items.title: Jensen Huang's Stunning Return as Nvidia CEO: A Timeline of Events

items.summary: The Nvidia board reinstated Jensen Huang to the CEO position, a move that boosted Nvidia's share price by about a third. According to the article, this decision followed a phone call from someone in the White House—possibly Donald Trump himself—who reportedly told the board there was nothing to worry about regarding stories concerning Huang's relationship with Alice Huang and an alleged connection to China. The article draws parallels between Huang's reinstatement and Sam Altman being fired by OpenAI only to be reinstated within weeks following investor pressure, suggesting Silicon Valley has developed a tendency to treat company founders as untouchable figures. Trump stated that the board asked whether there was a national security problem and he responded 'No, it's not a problem.' The article frames this episode as evidence of growing corporate power in the AI era, comparing current tech leaders—described as Huangs, Altmans, Musks, Amodeis, and Zuckerbergs—to Gilded Age industrialists like Vanderbilt, Carnegie, Rockefeller, and Morgan. It notes that during 1913, the richest 1% of taxpayers drew almost 18% of the nation's income and held nearly 40% of the nation's wealth—shares similar to what they hold today—and by the late 1970s this figure had fallen below a quarter. The article references President Rutherford B. Hayes writing in his diary that 'This is a government of corporations, by corporations, and for corporations,' echoing Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg address.
items.title: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after White House intervention

items.summary: According to a Wall Street Journal report, Nvidia's co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang admitted before the company's board that he had more than three alleged affairs beyond those already reported. The 63-year-old reportedly expressed regret over his behavior during Sunday's lengthy board meeting, in which members spoke with him for several hours about undisclosed private relationships and explained the importance of transparency and honesty. Although these claims have not been independently verified, the board decided on Monday to reinstate Huang as CEO. The dispute reportedly began when reports emerged that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, an official at Singapore's Megaspeed company who U.S. authorities accuse of spying for China; China has dismissed those accusations as baseless. Earlier reporting by the New York Times and Reuters also raised questions about other alleged private relationships involving Huang. Following his reinstatement announcement on Monday, Nvidia employees greeted him with applause in a video from its headquarters in Santa Clara, California, while an online petition supporting his return reportedly gathered thousands of signatures. The report claims that U.S. President Donald Trump and several tech-industry figures backed the decision to bring Huang back.
items.title: Nvidia Board Reinstates Jensen Huang After Private-Relationship Confession, Shares Jump

A TSMC unit filed with Texas officials on Nov. 24 that a property tax abatement would be the deciding factor in whether it builds a $22.6 billion chip manufacturing facility in Brazos County, according to a document filed with the state comptroller's office. Arizona remains a rival site for the project, per the filing.

The proposed facility would include one or more chip fabrication plants and support infrastructure on more than 3,200 acres in the county. It is projected to manufacture chips using 2-nanometer or more advanced technology for AI, high performance computing, and mobile devices. The company submitted its application under Texas's Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation (JETI) program through the Comptroller of Public Accounts.

TSMC noted that expanding in Arizona—where it has operated a semiconductor manufacturing plant since late 2024—may offer certain operational and economic advantages. However, the company stated that the requested tax limitation dictates whether TSMC commits to building the project in Texas. The facility is projected to create at least 2,099 direct jobs over the next four decades, according to the filing.
items.title: TSMC Unit Requests Texas Property Tax Limit for $22.6 Billion Chip Facility

items.summary: An author presents a personal list ranking the best fiction books of 2026, ordered by reading sequence. The selections include Siri Hustvedt's 'Ghost Stories: A Memoir,' Karl Knausgaard's 'The School of Night,' Juan Marsé's newly translated 'Last Evenings with Teresa,' Claudia Piñeiro's 'Cathedrals,' Christian Kracht's 2025 novel 'Eurotrash' and his forthcoming 2026 work 'Air,' Munir Hachemi's 'The Mulai,' Olga Grjasnowa's 'My Dreadful Body,' China Mieville's still-unfinished 'The Rouse,' the German-language edition of Ingeborg Bachmann and Max Frisch's correspondence, Adolfo Bioy Casares' newly translated 'Morel's Invention' by Margaret Jull Costa, Missouri Williams' 'The Vivisectors,' Mathias Enard's 'Perfecting the Shot,' M. John Harrison's 'The End of Everything,' Solvej Ball's fifth volume in a series that cannot be started at book five, and forthcoming works from Min Lee and Jon Fosse that remain unread. The author identifies Knausgaard's novel, the Bachmann-Frisch correspondence, and Bioy Casares' work as standout titles for a 'best of.' Reflecting on the literary landscape, the author expresses belief that high-quality fiction is becoming increasingly important and notes satisfaction with how writers and translators are responding.
items.title: Author Shares Best Fiction of 2026

items.summary: A study titled 'The Health Effects of Eating Red Meat,' subtitled 'Natural Experiment in Alpha-Gal Syndrome,' used national electronic health records to compare changes in weight and cardiometabolic health over two years before and after newly detected alpha-gal syndrome with those in patients who had other tick-borne diseases. The authors note that observational associations between red meat consumption and cardiometabolic disease are confounded by diet and other health behaviors, so they used a comparison group of patients bitten by ticks but whose diagnoses carry no dietary restriction.
items.title: Alpha-Gal Syndrome Linked to Modest Cardiometabolic Benefits in Natural Experiment Study

items.summary:
Donald Trump reportedly made up to $15m (£11.5m) on his Nvidia holdings after the chipmaker's shares surged following the reinstatement of co-founder Jensen Huang as chief executive, according to a report by The Item. Huang was ousted from Nvidia in 2024 amid allegations involving three affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with employees, but the board brought him back after an intervention Trump described on CNBC as convincing them he "made the deal." Financial disclosures filed with the Office of Government Ethics indicate Trump may have owned up to 370,000 Nvidia shares as of September 30, per data first reported by the Financial Times. The president's holdings in Nvidia range between $23m and $86m over two years according to a BBC review; he has sold part of his stake since returning to office and gained between $3.5m and $10.2m on those trades, per government disclosures.

Nvidia shares jumped 31.5% in Monday's trading, adding roughly $950bn to the company's value as Huang returned to Santa Clara headquarters amid a crowd of employees chanting his name. The rally extended across Asia-Pacific markets Tuesday: Taiwan's TW50 index rose 9.5%, South Korea's Kospi climbed 6.5% led by SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, and Japan's Nikkei gained nearly 4%, while European markets were broadly flat. Nvidia shares then fell 4.1% in premarket trading to $158.26 as traders weighed political backlash over Huang's return; US markets are expected to open slightly lower Tuesday after Monday's gains.

The volatility reflects broader AI-sector concerns about high debt levels funding infrastructure buildouts and potential tougher regulation following the Democrats' midterm victory. Senator Ruben Gallego (D-Arizona) called for an investigation into stock positions before Huang's announcement, calling the White House "the most corrupt in history" and suggesting Trump may have started popping the AI bubble; Roger Lee of Cavendish questioned whether technology CEOs like Huang are now too systemically important to be fired. Economists noted Huang's return reduced fears of an imminent AI-bubble burst, making a rate hike more likely: Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid said markets were once again pricing in a 25 basis point Federal Reserve increase at the December meeting.
items.title: Trump Made Up to $15m on Nvidia Stock After Jensen Huang's Return

items.summary: Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia CEO, an event that became the top trending post on Weibo and is being described by some observers as one of the greatest U-turns of all time. Chinese state media dismissed claims that a woman connected to Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security as a spy, framing the saga instead as a smear campaign orchestrated by China hawks in Washington; The Global Times called it a 'witch hunt.' Meanwhile, the White House and President Donald Trump have said Huang poses no national security threat, though investigations into the allegations remain ongoing. Observers note that Huang's reappointment came shortly after Xi Jinping met with Trump in Shenzhen last week, raising questions about whether direct engagement influences Washington; Trump confirmed the two discussed Huang but did not elaborate further, while Beijing has not commented. The episode reinforced a view among Chinese officials of two camps in Washington regarding export controls on advanced technology. Although Huang argues that US restrictions will push firms like Huawei to build independent alternatives, his return is seen as no guarantee of relief for China because chip sales remain contentious ahead of an expected Trump-Xi meeting in December. New rules from the Bureau of Industry and Security are tightening restrictions by targeting not only direct exports but also Chinese firms' ability to use computing power overseas through cloud providers in countries like Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand; China has yet to react with measures of its own. Investors will watch for escalation that could weigh on US equity markets, as Trump's willingness to intervene in Nvidia's leadership decisions is seen by some observers as leverage given his concern about the stock market. Trump has personally invested in Nvidia, though the White House emphasized he placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons. China previously used its rare earth metals chokehold to bring the US to trade negotiations; if chip export restrictions and Chinese retaliation escalate, that could affect markets because American companies rely on rare earths for products from cars to defense systems. Observers note more trouble lies ahead as China pursues what it describes as a 'constructive strategic relationship' with the US over control of critical technology and minerals affecting military influence and economic power. Huang is set to testify before Congress next month, and a Democrat-controlled Congress will raise pressure in January; Arkansas senator Tom Cotton wrote on X that the Nvidia controversy 'is just the tip of the iceberg.'
items.title: Jensen Huang's Return to Nvidia CEO Role Sparks Reflections in China

items.summary: On November 23, Nvidia's board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate co-founder Jensen Huang as president and chief executive officer effective immediately, reinstating him as a board member after reversing its earlier decision on his departure. The company said the board was satisfied with Huang's candor and leadership capabilities during discussions that followed his resignation, and it consulted senior US government officials before concluding his return posed no national security risk. Board Chair Harvey C. Jones stated Huang is the right person to lead Nvidia and that reinstatement serves shareholders, employees, partners and customers; he will remain board chair while Colette Kress continues as chief financial officer after serving as interim CEO during Huang's absence. Huang had voluntarily resigned on November 12 after the board raised concerns about his personal conduct being inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and corporate culture. On Nvidia's quarterly earnings call on November 17, Jones said the board unanimously accepted the resignation and did not intend to reinstate Huang, prompting Kress to become interim CEO as the company searched for a permanent successor. The reversal followed public support for Huang's return, including a Reuters report that a petition had attracted more than 180,000 signatures with one from Tesla CEO Elon Musk, while President Donald Trump—who urged Nvidia to bring Huang back—welcomed the decision on Truth Social and said the US government saw no national security risk. Despite his return, an independent investigation launched by the board will continue through completion with Huang pledging full cooperation; Nvidia has also established a separate National Security and Export Control Committee of independent directors overseeing trade compliance while seeking to appoint a chief compliance officer.
items.title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO After Board Reversal

items.summary: US President Donald Trump said he spoke directly with Nvidia's board before the reinstatement of chief executive Jensen Huang, who had resigned less than two weeks earlier amid a scandal involving an alleged affair with a woman suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence. In an interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump explained that he contacted board members because he considered Nvidia strategically important to the United States and described finding "the board to be very, very reasonable." Separately, Nvidia announced on Monday that its board had unanimously voted to reinstate Huang as president and CEO, effective immediately. The decision followed an initial statement from the board indicating it did not intend to bring Huang back, despite his expressed willingness to return.
items.title: Nvidia Board Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO After Trump Intervention

items.summary:
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO on Monday, just 11 days after being ousted over a spy scandal. The event underlined his apparently indispensable role in an industry that has fueled a tech revolution and global economic boom.

Huang founded Nvidia three decades ago with two friends in a Silicon Valley diner to solve problems normal computers couldn't handle using powerful semiconductors, including 3D graphics processing units (GPUs). The company created the first GPU in 1999, capitalizing on growth in video games, data centres, cloud computing and generative AI. Nvidia has become one of the world's most valuable companies due to demand for these chips.

The scandal that forced his resignation on 12 November involved revelations he cheated on his wife with a woman who US officials believe had links to Chinese intelligence. Huang holds roughly a 4% stake in the company and is worth around $160 billion (€138bn), according to Forbes, making him one of the world's richest people.

Huang has become a close informal adviser on AI to Donald Trump, travelling with the US president on Air Force One to Beijing earlier this year. He emerged as a high-profile entrepreneur drawing stadium crowds presenting cutting-edge components essential to developing AI tools like ChatGPT. On visits to his native Taiwan he is received like a megastar.

Huang was born in Taipei in 1963 and sent away at nine years old with his brother to boarding school in Kentucky, recommended by his uncle as prestigious but actually a school for troubled youth; too young to be a student there, he boarded while attending a nearby public school alongside children of tobacco farmers. With poor English he was bullied and forced to clean toilets, though he later said "the ending of the story is I loved the time I was there." His parents had by then settled in Oregon's northwestern US state.

He graduated from university at just 20 (per Forbes) before joining AMD and LSI Logic to design chips. He has rejected calls to deliberately slow down AI development even as some insiders warn the technology could threaten human existence within a decade, telling CBS News in September that "we should go as fast as we can" on AI.
items.title: Jensen Huang's Rise and Dramatic Return as Nvidia CEO

items.summary: The Trump administration added Singapore-based Megaspeed International to the Commerce Department's entity list, barring it from purchasing advanced AI chips without a U.S. license and targeting the firm at the center of allegations that Jensen Huang lost his job at Nvidia Corp over an affair with Alice Huang, who is suspected of spying for China. The Monday filing formally placed the company established by Alice Huang on the blacklist while also naming a Singapore-based unit of Alibaba Group Holding; Alibaba denied it had ever diverted restricted semiconductors. Revelations this month about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang renewed scrutiny over whether Megaspeed smuggled Nvidia AI chips into China and raised questions about Commerce's enforcement of export controls designed to keep sensitive technology from adversaries.
items.title: U.S. Blacklists Megaspeed After Nvidia Spy Scandal

items.summary:
According to Vivek Mahajan, chief technology officer of Tokyo-based Fujitsu, initial demand for the company's new Monaka server chips is exceeding expectations. The 2-nanometer processors use Arm Holdings architecture and are named after a traditional Japanese confectionery. Shortly after commercial sales began this month, Mahajan said Fujitsu was already in discussions with manufacturer Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company about securing enough production capacity.

Mahajan attributed the demand to growing interest in sovereign data security across defense, finance, manufacturing, and public sectors among customers in Japan, the U.S., and Europe. He noted that most of the 45 companies that received Monaka product samples in August are likely to place orders. Fujitsu has historically restricted use of its processors to its own systems, such as for the Fugaku supercomputer, but with Monaka it seeks to sell chips to other server makers.

Mahajan warned that supply constraints could arise if demand outpaces current estimates of about 500,000 units in sales over two years. He explained that a single manufacturer shipping roughly 30,000 servers would require more than 200,000 Monaka chips.

Fujitsu supplies the Japanese government with computing, AI, networking, and security products. The company expects Monaka to generate ¥35 billion ($220 million) in sales next fiscal year, with annual sales reaching ¥500 billion by 2035 — a target Mahajan said could be hit two years earlier.

Analysts on average expect Fujitsu's revenue to stay flat this fiscal year through March at ¥3.6 trillion, and about 5% growth each year through 2030. In the broader market, Intel and Advanced Micro Devices dominate server CPUs but face pressure from Arm-based chips and Nvidia, which touts energy efficiency. Mahajan said Monaka targets companies' needs for better performance, memory access, security, and energy efficiency.

Mahajan emphasized Fujitsu's competitive position: "We are the only ones in Japan that make a CPU today and probably only ones outside the U.S. that make such a cutting-edge CPU." He called it an alternative customers can use against U.S. and Chinese suppliers.
items.title: Fujitsu's Fujitsu-Monaka CPUs Face Supply Shortages Amid Surging Demand for U.S.-China Chip Alternatives

items.summary:
A nuclear explosion in space would be unlikely to cause widespread injuries on Earth but could disable satellites that provide services people depend on daily, including some that save lives. In the United States, satellite failures could make it harder for emergency crews to communicate in remote areas; if GPS were also disrupted, drivers and pilots could lose navigation guidance, and financial networks could lose a source of precise time.

History provides evidence because such an explosion has already occurred. On July 8, 1962, the United States detonated a nuclear weapon about 400 kilometers (250 miles) above the Pacific in the Starfish Prime test; people in Hawaii held "watch-the-bomb parties" and followed the countdown on shortwave radio before the night sky lit up. An electromagnetic pulse knocked out some streetlights in Hawaii, some Pacific radio links briefly went down, and although the glow faded within minutes, some satellites failed months later.

The physics of an explosion differs in space because the air is too thin for a conventional fireball to form or for a destructive shock wave to reach the ground. Charged particles made denser air below glow, creating an artificial aurora, and the atmosphere absorbed much of the initial radiation. Satellites are especially vulnerable because they orbit above most of the atmosphere that shields people on the ground from the initial radiation.

In orbit, the initial burst of X-rays can damage spacecraft right away, but Earth's magnetic field can also trap electrons released after the blast as it did after Starfish Prime; satellites receive another dose each time they cross the resulting radiation belt. Over time, that exposure can damage electronics and solar panels. GPS satellites send signals that help phones, planes and ships work out where they are; they orbit about 20,200 kilometers above Earth and could keep working even if satellites closer to Earth failed.

But satellites do different jobs: a ship's emergency beacon can use GPS to work out its location, then send it to rescuers through a separate satellite network, so if part of that network failed the alert could take longer to get through. Which systems would be exposed depends on where the explosion happened and which satellites crossed the radiation belt.

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars parties from placing nuclear weapons in orbit, and the 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty prohibits its parties from carrying out nuclear explosions in space. The Outer Space Treaty has no dedicated system for checking what spacecraft carry; a detonation is easier to detect because US satellite sensors are designed to pick up the signals it gives off.

The United States could protect itself through shielding that might help protect satellite electronics and backups that could keep some services running, though during a GPS outage pilots over the contiguous US can use ground-based navigation aids. Operators could launch replacements, but those satellites could still face lingering radiation or debris; radiation could leave many satellites intact but unable to steer, and if two objects collided fragments from the crash could hit other satellites, creating more debris and triggering further collisions that could continue on their own as Kessler syndrome. Whether an explosion would trigger such a cascade is uncertain, though if it did the debris could endanger replacement satellites for years.

Some radioactive particles could enter the atmosphere and eventually settle on the ground from a space blast, but because the explosion is too far away to sweep up the soil and water that carry fallout from a surface explosion, the concentrated local fallout that can expose people near a ground-level blast to high doses would be unlikely. As the particles disperse their radioactivity decreases over time.
items.title: What Happens If a Nuclear Weapon Explodes in Space?

items.summary: Michael Radomiljac, 48, was found guilty after a six-day trial in the Busselton District Court on five counts of rape, one count of strangulation and one count of illegally detaining his former partner Kelly North. The abuse occurred during their relationship spanning late 2024 and early 2025. Radomiljac was found not guilty of one count of rape while another charge was discontinued. Prosecutor Samuel Lindsay described him as an 'ogre' in closing arguments, acknowledging the case relied largely on Ms North's testimony. The prosecution alleged he forced her into scalding hot showers before sexually assaulting her, detained her for three hours at his house and vehicle in December 2024, and choked and raped her during a March 2025 weekend getaway after accusing her of an affair. Medical examinations found bruises consistent with strangulation and extensive genital bruising. Ms North initially spoke out last year when Radomiljac was released on bail without an ankle tracker. Defence counsel Tony Hager characterised the relationship as toxic, marred by drug use and jealousy, arguing that apologetic texts were not admissions of guilt and that he is 'not a rapist.' Radomiljac has been remanded in custody and will be sentenced next month.
items.title: West Australian Man Convicted of Raping, Choking Former Partner

items.summary:
Researchers in Indonesian Borneo have observed that gibbons' morning songs have been reduced or absent during this fire season, a pattern also seen following forest fires in the same area in 2006. The Borneo Nature Foundation field team in Sebangau, Central Kalimantan, reports that on days when haze is thick, gibbons sing less; their songs sound shorter and morning duets start later than usual or do not happen at all. Susan Cheyne, BNF's co-director and vice-chair of the IUCN Primate Specialist Group Section on Small Apes, documented a similar pattern after 2006 fires but noted that researchers have yet to formally analyze this year's findings until fieldwork can resume once the fires subside.

Singing plays a central role in gibbon social and reproductive life: these territorial, socially monogamous primates sing to attract mates and defend territory through elaborate duets. Cheyne describes their songs as an "honest signal biologically," since complex synchronized duets are difficult to fake and indicate healthy, bonded pairs. Gibbon vocal behavior is also sensitive to environmental conditions; research has found they sing less when exposed to disturbances like rain and noise pollution.

Since mid-September, air quality in Central Kalimantan frequently reached hazardous levels, with Palangkaraya peaking at 11,981 — nearly four times the level the U.S. Air Quality Index classifies as hazardous (4.0). As of Nov. 2, the Indonesian Ministry of Health reported more than 400,000 cases of acute respiratory infections across Central Kalimantan and six other affected provinces.

Cheyne believes smoke is a major driver behind reduced singing: it irritates gibbons' airways like humans exposed to high concentrations of smoke particles. "I'm sure an opera singer would never be able to hit the notes and range and frequency that they should be able to if they're constantly breathing in smoke," she says.

Smoke may also reduce visibility by dimming forest light, delaying duets around sunrise when gibbons typically sing as light filters through the canopy. An analysis of more than 300 days of gibbon singing data from northern Lao PDR found gibbons tend to sing later and less often on foggy mornings (White et al., American Journal of Primatology, 86(11), e23679). Cheyne says light is the main cue. Gibbons also perform a visual, acrobatic territorial display while swinging and singing simultaneously.

Alasdair Owens, a post-graduate researcher at the University of Exeter studying Bornean white-bearded gibbons (Hylobates albibarbis), says food availability may become more evident in coming months. Fires have burned across parts of gibbon ranges, including an estimated 13,000 hectares (32,100 acres) inside Sebangau National Park; previous El Niño fires led to "almost famine conditions" in the forest.

A 2015 study on orangutans found females adjusted behavior for months after forest fires and fruit shortages — resting more and traveling less (Ashbury et al., International Journal of Primatology, 43(2), 189-215). Gibbons have also been found to sing less when food availability declines. The longer-term effects on gibbon health, social relationships, and reproductive success remain unclear; Cheyne predicts that if families sing less, neighbors might encroach on territory causing conflict between groups while young gibbons struggle to find mates.

Reduced active hours from haze and delayed duets could also have far-reaching consequences: gibbons may have less time to feed and socialize. Less singing complicates research because scientists typically rely on acoustic data to locate and count animals by triangulating sound from listening posts; Owens says how many times a group calls matters less than whether it calls at all, so researchers will need longer surveys.

Owens is developing an automated method using passive acoustic monitoring and deep learning with GPS-synchronized recorders. By comparing the time a call takes to reach each device, he calculates location "quite high accuracy," 20 meters (66 feet) in the best cases; he hopes to test this in 2027 across unprotected and secondary forest in Central Kalimantan.

In Sebangau, BNF plans to return to gibbon families monitored for 20 years once it is safe, following groups and listening for calls while using triangulation to confirm territory occupation. The team also plans to work with park authorities to survey population density across Sebangau National Park by combining acoustic monitoring and line transect data.

Cheyne says comparing this year's findings with previous haze seasons could help establish whether repeated seasons have a cumulative effect on gibbon health and breeding.
items.title: Borneo Gibbon Singing Declines as Smoke Silences Forests During Fire Season

He noted that for far too long the abundance of natural resources has contrasted with the meager benefits derived by Congolese people, as minerals have been exported while much of their economic value was created elsewhere abroad. Tshisekedi said the country must no longer be merely a major producer of minerals but instead become an economy capable of taking greater control over processing and value creation. He called for moving beyond simply extracting resources to develop domestic capacity to process them locally.
items.title: DRC President Calls for Local Processing of Mineral Wealth

items.summary: A fire broke out on November 21 at the Fonusa Agung Mulia factory in Banten province, west of Jakarta. Aerial footage filmed Monday shows collapsed roofs and large sections of the complex reduced to ruins. The death toll has risen to 26, with eight workers still missing; most victims were recovered from the second floor, where rescuers said many had died trying to reach an emergency exit. More than 600 emergency personnel have been mobilised, though unstable structures are hampering searches across the roughly 2,000-square-metre area affected by the blaze. Police are collecting DNA samples from relatives to identify victims. Preliminary reports suggest an electrical fault in an air-conditioning unit may have sparked the fire, although the cause remains unconfirmed.
items.title: Indonesia: Search continues for workers trapped after deadly factory fire

items.summary: Two people were injured and a 17-year-old student was arrested after an alleged school shooting at the First Technical School in Kragujevac on Tuesday morning. According to police and Serbia's Interior Ministry, the incident occurred around 8 am local time (0700 GMT), roughly 140 kilometers (87 miles) south of Belgrade. The teenager allegedly fired a small-caliber rifle in the school's entrance hall; one person sustained a gunshot wound while another was injured by shattered glass from the discharge, and both were reported as not being in life-threatening condition. Local media reported that the firearm malfunctioned after firing, which allowed police to intervene and arrest the suspect at the scene.
items.title: Two Injured in School Shooting in Serbia, Teenage Suspect Arrested

items.summary: Mexico's traditional 'P'urepecha Ball' game attracted interest as the first edition of the Ethnosport Culture Festival was held outside Türkiye, taking place for the first time in Riyadh. Organized as part of Riyadh Season under Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030, the festival introduced visitors to an ancient Mexican sport whose origins date back to 1500 BC (approximately 3,500 years ago). The game is played on a field about 120 meters long and 6-8 meters wide by teams of 6 players each. Manuel Sanchez, leader of the P'urepecha Ball team, told Anadolu that representing Mexico far from home was meaningful and that the festival helped gain recognition for preserving their culture beyond national borders. He noted the sport belongs to the hockey family, originated in Michoacan state's earliest inhabitants, is also known as 'Uarhukua Ch'anakua,' and has its oldest traces discovered at Cerro de los Penoles with depictions of players using sticks and spectators watching. Sanchez said visitors were particularly fascinated by a performance involving a ball set on fire, which he described as celebrating life while paying tribute to death, tied to the god Curicaveri and the cultural importance of sun and fire. The team has competed internationally for 21 years, including at the 4th World Nomad Games in Iznik, Türkiye in 2022, Brazil's first Indigenous Peoples' Gathering, and Italy's Tocatì Festival in 2012 and 2014.
items.title: Mexico's P'urepecha Ball Game Draws Interest at Ethnosport Culture Festival in Saudi Arabia

items.summary:
The article argues that Africa's Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) and related free-trade policies remain largely blind to the small cross-border traders who move goods between countries, link local markets, and sustain household incomes. These informal traders—who buy in one country and resell in another using personal relationships—fall squarely within the AfCFTA's scope of creating a borderless market that would boost intra-African trade, promote economic transformation, and help millions escape poverty, yet they are still largely absent from integration policies.

The argument gains urgency amid falling international aid: the OECD reported in June 2026 that official development assistance fell 23.3% globally in 2025 and projected a further 6.9% decline in 2026, making it more pressing for African countries to strengthen economic activity and expand access to regional markets rather than replace aid with trade.

The author's research focuses on marginalized actors—small businesses, cross-border trade, and diaspora networks—in Africa. The piece contends that the continent cannot realize its commercial integration ambitions while public policies and official statistics continue to overlook informal traders' economic contribution; it argues the free-trade agreement would be more inclusive if it gave greater weight to informal traders' realities rather than prioritizing established firms and large operations.

Informal cross-border trade is substantial but poorly measured. The UN Economic Commission for Africa estimates African informal cross-border trade at between $10 billion and $24 billion annually, while the author's research suggests these traders account for roughly 30% to 72% of formal trade among neighboring African countries; a separate regional estimate places Southern African Development Community informal cross-border trade at $17.6 billion. Women make up about 70% of the traders. These figures are estimates rather than precise measurements, since informal activity is hard to measure consistently and varies by country, goods, and methods.

The statistics gap matters because unmeasured transactions risk causing policymakers to underestimate how interdependent economies within a region already are; accurate data would help them calibrate border infrastructure, tariff regimes, and support services to actual trade volumes. For many women and young people the activity offers an entrepreneurship path when formal jobs are scarce, generating income by buying goods at lower prices across borders and reselling locally while creating jobs for transporters, handlers, and merchants.

The informal sector also poses problems: some traders evade taxes or bypass customs obligations, and others work in precarious conditions vulnerable to exploitation. The author notes that understanding why the activity persists can help policymakers find solutions without undermining those who depend on it.

AfCFTA offers an opportunity to extend trade and deepen regional economic integration by reducing border crossing times, simplifying customs procedures, harmonizing product controls, and building shared infrastructure—but lowering barriers for firms does not automatically improve access for small traders. These traders still face complex customs procedures, unpredictable requirements, corruption, harassment, and limited access to affordable financing, which can make formal trade circuits costly or impractical given their low capital.

This creates a paradox: the traders already help link African markets, yet rules designed to facilitate regional trade often ignore their daily realities. The author proposes three concrete changes—first, governments and regional institutions should make commercial information and border procedures more accessible through clear customs guidance, simplified processes for eligible small shipments, and stronger protections against harassment; second, African countries need more reliable and complete data by harmonizing measurement methods drawing on the African Union Commission, Afreximbank, and the UN Economic Commission for Africa to understand what is traded, where economic activity occurs, and which traders face the biggest obstacles; third, traders themselves should be involved in trade-policy design through associations representing small traders, including women traders, who can help identify wasteful procedures and needed protections.

The author cautions that formalizing informal cross-border trade must proceed carefully: simply requiring compliance with complex procedures could exclude some traders. Governments would instead benefit from mechanisms allowing gradual integration into formal trade, with rules adapted to each trader's activity size and characteristics; tailored financial services such as digital payments and accessible credit could also help.

Finally, the author stresses that informal cross-border trade cannot by itself solve Africa's broader development-financing challenges nor eliminate the need for international cooperation, public investment, or effective institutions. But African countries do not need to build regional economic links from scratch—many already exist through traders who move goods, generate income, and connect communities across national borders—and better assessment of this activity, more accessible border procedures, and constructive engagement with traders would strengthen regional integration in service of the populations it is meant to benefit.
items.title: Why Free-Trade Policies Must Adapt to African Cross-Border Traders
